concepts.name: Squares near a base
concepts.description: For a number close to 100 (or 50, or 1000), the square is (number + surplus) followed by the surplus squared, written with as many digits as the base has zeros.

concepts.name: Squares by splitting
concepts.description: Split a number into a round part and a small part and use (a ± b)² = a² ± 2ab + b². From a known square, the next one is n² + n + (n + 1).

concepts.name: Cubes of two-digit numbers
concepts.description: For 10a + b, write a³, a²b, ab², b³ in a row (each term is the last times b ÷ a), double the middle two and add the columns with carries.

concepts.name: Square roots of perfect squares
concepts.description: The unit digit of a perfect square narrows its root to one or two last digits; the part left after dropping two digits gives the tens part; (10k + 5)² decides between two candidates.

concepts.name: Cube roots of perfect cubes
concepts.description: Every unit digit of a cube comes from exactly one digit (2 ↔ 8 and 3 ↔ 7 swap, the rest stay). The part left after dropping three digits fixes the tens digit.

concepts.name: Roots of decimals and fractions
concepts.description: A square root halves the number of decimal places (count them in pairs); a cube root divides it by three. For fractions, take the root of the top and the bottom.

concepts.name: Roots of non-perfect squares
concepts.description: Take the nearest perfect square a² and use √N ≈ a + (N − a²) ÷ 2a. The estimate is slightly high, and very good when N is close to a².

concepts.name: Perfect-square tests
concepts.description: A perfect square never ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8, ends in an even number of zeros, has a digital root of 1, 4, 7 or 9, and if it ends in 5 it ends in 25.

formulas.title: Squares near 100 and 50
formulas.prompt: How do you square a number close to 100 or to 50 in your head?
formulas.formula:
Near 100: n² = (n + d) | d², d = n − 100, d² as two digits
Near 50: n² = (25 + d) | d², d = n − 50

variables.meaning: the surplus over the base (negative for a deficit)

formulas.commonMistake: Writing d² with too few digits: 97² is 94 | 09 = 9,409, not 949.

formulas.title: Squares near 1000
formulas.prompt: How do you square a number close to 1,000?
formulas.formula: n² = (n + d) | d², with d² written as three digits
formulas.explanation: The base has three zeros, so the right part holds three digits. Pad with zeros, and carry if d² reaches 1,000.

formulas.title: Square by splitting
formulas.prompt: How do you square a number that is near a round number but not near a base?
formulas.formula:
(a ± b)² = a² ± 2ab + b²
Choose a round, b small
formulas.explanation: Squaring a round number is easy, the middle term is one multiplication, and b² is tiny. Pick whichever split makes the numbers friendliest.
formulas.commonMistake: Dropping the middle term: (70 − 2)² is not 4,900 − 4.

formulas.title: The next square from a known one
formulas.prompt: You know n². How do you get (n + 1)² instantly?
formulas.explanation: Consecutive squares differ by the sum of the two numbers: (n + 1)² − n² = 2n + 1 = n + (n + 1).
formulas.commonMistake: Adding 2n only and forgetting the extra 1.

formulas.title: Cube of a two-digit number
formulas.prompt: How do you cube a two-digit number such as 12 or 23 without long multiplication?
formulas.formula:
(10a + b)³: row a³ | a²b | ab² | b³
Add 2a²b and 2ab² under the middle two, then add the columns from the right with carries
formulas.explanation: It is (a + b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³ laid out by place value. Each term in the row is the previous one times b ÷ a, so the row is quick to write.
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting to triple the middle terms (adding the doubled row only once).

formulas.title: Square root of a perfect square
formulas.prompt: How do you find the square root of a four- or five-digit perfect square quickly?
formulas.formula:
1. Unit digit → one or two possible last digits of the root
2. Drop the last two digits → largest k with k² ≤ what is left
3. Two candidates? Compare with (10k + 5)²
formulas.explanation: The root of a number between (10k)² and (10k + 10)² lies between 10k and 10k + 10. The midpoint square (10k + 5)² splits the candidates 10k + small and 10k + large.
formulas.commonMistake: Picking a candidate without the midpoint check (77 instead of 73).

formulas.title: Last digits of square roots
formulas.prompt: A perfect square ends in 1, 4, 5, 6, 9 or 0. Which digits can its root end in?
formulas.explanation: d and 10 − d have squares with the same unit digit, so most square endings come from two root endings. 5 and 0 come from one each.
formulas.commonMistake: Thinking a square ending in 6 must have a root ending in 6 (64² = 4,096).
formulas.applicationPrompt: Which digits can the root of 2,304 end in?

formulas.title: Cube root of a perfect cube
formulas.prompt: How do you find the cube root of a perfect cube of up to six digits?
formulas.formula:
1. Unit digit of the cube → unit digit of the root (2 ↔ 8, 3 ↔ 7, others unchanged)
2. Drop the last three digits → largest k with k³ ≤ what is left
formulas.explanation: Cubes of 0 to 9 all end in different digits, so the unit digit is never ambiguous. The leading part sits between k³ and (k + 1)³, which fixes the tens digit.
formulas.commonMistake: Taking the root of the cube’s unit digit as itself for 2, 3, 7, 8 (a cube ending in 8 has a root ending in 2).

formulas.title: Roots of decimals and fractions
formulas.prompt: How do you take the square root (or cube root) of a decimal or a fraction?
formulas.formula:
√: pair the decimal places (the root has half as many)
∛: group them in threes (a third as many)
√(a/b) = √a ÷ √b
formulas.explanation: 0.0169 = 169 ÷ 10⁴, so its root is 13 ÷ 10² = 0.13. The number of decimal places must be even for a square root (a multiple of 3 for a cube root); add a zero if needed.
formulas.commonMistake: Keeping the same number of decimal places: √0.0169 is not 0.0013.

formulas.title: Square root of a non-perfect square
formulas.prompt: How do you estimate √N when N is not a perfect square?
formulas.formula: √N ≈ a + (N − a²) ÷ 2a, where a² is the perfect square nearest N
formulas.explanation: If √N = a + x with x small, then N = a² + 2ax + x² ≈ a² + 2ax, so x ≈ (N − a²) ÷ 2a. It also works with a² above N (the correction is then negative).
formulas.commonMistake: Dividing by a instead of 2a, which doubles the correction.

formulas.title: Tests a perfect square must pass
formulas.prompt: How can you tell at a glance that a number is NOT a perfect square?
formulas.formula:
A perfect square:
• never ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8
• ends in an even number of zeros
• has digital root 1, 4, 7 or 9
• ending in 5 → ends in 25
formulas.explanation: Each test is a property of every square, so failing any one proves the number is not a square. Passing all of them does not prove that it is.
formulas.example:
4,762 ends in 2 → not a square
6,241 passes every test, and it is 79²
formulas.commonMistake: Treating "passes the tests" as "is a square": 1,111 ends in 1 and has digital root 4, but it is not a square.

levels.title: Squares From a Base, Roots From the Ends
levels.description: Square numbers near 100 in one line, split awkward numbers, and read a square root off the two ends of a number.

blocks.title: Square from the nearest base
blocks.body:
92 is 8 below 100. Take 8 off 92 to get 84, then write 8² = 64 after it: 92² = 8,464.

Above the base the same rule adds: 107 → 107 + 7 = 114, then 49 → 11,449. The right part always has as many digits as the base has zeros.

blocks.title: Base 100
blocks.caption: d is the surplus over 100 (negative for a deficit). Near 50 use 25 + d for the left part.

blocks.title: Split when no base is near
Read a square root off the ends
blocks.body: A perfect square’s last digit narrows its root to at most two last digits. The digits before the last two narrow it to a ten. Between the two candidates, the square of the number ending in 5 decides.
This topic builds on the must-know squares and cubes tables. Knowing squares to 30 and cubes to 15 by heart makes every bracket step instant.

levels.title: Squares, Cubes and Roots Formulas
levels.description: Base squares, splitting, the cube row and the root methods.

levels.title: Direct Squares and Roots
levels.description: One-step squares, roots and square tests.

levels.title: Bigger Numbers, Same Methods
levels.description: Five-digit roots, cubes by the row method and base 1,000.

levels.title: Roots in Problems
levels.description: Large bases, six-digit squares and roots inside area and volume problems.

levels.title: Mixed Squares, Cubes and Roots Practice
Advanced: Decimals, Estimates and Square Tests
levels.description: Roots of decimals and fractions, estimating roots that are not whole, and proving a number is not a square.

blocks.title: Decimal places come in pairs
blocks.body:
0.0169 is 169 ÷ 10,000. Its square root is 13 ÷ 100 = 0.13: four decimal places became two. For a cube root they come in threes: ∛0.008 = 0.2.

For fractions, root the top and the bottom: √(6¼) = √(25/4) = 5/2.

blocks.title: Estimating a root
blocks.caption: a² is the nearest perfect square, above or below N. √70 ≈ 8 + 6 ÷ 16 = 8.375; the true value is 8.367.

blocks.title: Proving a number is not a square
blocks.body: Squares end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9; their zeros at the end come in pairs; their digital root is 1, 4, 7 or 9; and if they end in 5 they end in 25. Failing any one test settles it.
The tests can only rule a number out. 1,111 passes the last-digit and digital-root tests but is not a square (33² = 1,089, 34² = 1,156).

levels.title: Challenge: Roots Under Pressure
levels.description: Decimal and fraction roots, estimates and square tests.

questions.question: Using the base 100, find 96².
questions.explanation: 96 is 4 below 100. Left part: 96 − 4 = 92. Right part: 4² = 16. So 96² = 9,216.
questions.method: Number minus deficit | deficit squared.

hints.text: How far below 100 is 96?
Take the deficit off 96, then write 4² as two digits.

commonMistakes: Adding the deficit instead of subtracting it (100 | 16).

questions.question: What is √5,476?
questions.explanation: 5,476 ends in 6, so the root ends in 4 or 6. Dropping the last two digits leaves 54, and 7² = 49 ≤ 54 < 64, so the root is 74 or 76. 75² = 5,625 is more than 5,476, so the root is the smaller one: 74.
questions.method: Unit digit, bracket, midpoint.

hints.text: Which digits squared end in 6?
Compare 5,476 with 75² = 5,625.

commonMistakes: Choosing 76 by assuming a square ending in 6 has a root ending in 6.

questions.question: What is the cube root of 1,03,823?
questions.explanation: The cube ends in 3, so the root ends in 7 (7³ = 343). Dropping the last three digits leaves 103, and 4³ = 64 ≤ 103 < 125 = 5³, so the tens digit is 4. The root is 47.
questions.method: Unit digit, then the leading part.

hints.text: Which digit cubed ends in 3?
Drop the last three digits: between which two cubes does 103 lie?

commonMistakes: Thinking a cube ending in 3 has a root ending in 3.

questions.question: Which of these cannot be a perfect square?
questions.explanation: No perfect square ends in 8 (squares end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9), so 3,248 cannot be one. The others are squares: 67², 84² and 43².
questions.method: Check the last digit first.

hints.text: Which last digits can a perfect square have?
Look for an option ending in 2, 3, 7 or 8.

commonMistakes: Trying to find every root instead of testing the last digit.

questions.question: Which split gives 98² correctly and fastest?
questions.explanation: (a − b)² = a² − 2ab + b² with a = 100, b = 2 gives 10,000 − 400 + 4 = 9,604. The other options drop the middle term or halve it.
questions.method: Round number minus a small one, with the 2ab term.

hints.text: Which round number is 98 close to?
The middle term is 2 × 100 × 2.

commonMistakes: Forgetting the middle term 2ab.
Using ab instead of 2ab.

questions.question: Find 103² + 97².
questions.explanation: (100 + 3)² + (100 − 3)² = 2(100² + 3²) because the ±600 terms cancel. So the sum is 2 × 10,009 = 20,018.
questions.method: Pair the two squares so the middle terms cancel.

hints.text: Both numbers are 3 away from 100.
In (100 + 3)² + (100 − 3)² the middle terms cancel.

commonMistakes: Adding 10,609 and 9,409 with an arithmetic slip; the identity avoids it.

questions.question: Find 23³.
questions.explanation: Row for a = 2, b = 3: 8 | 12 | 18 | 27. Doubled middle terms 24 and 36 go underneath, giving columns 8 | 36 | 54 | 27. From the right: 27 → 7 carry 2; 54 + 2 = 56 → 6 carry 5; 36 + 5 = 41 → 1 carry 4; 8 + 4 = 12. So 23³ = 12,167.
questions.method: Row method for (10a + b)³.

hints.text: Start the row with a³ = 8 and multiply by 3/2 each step.
Triple the middle terms (row plus the doubled line), then carry.

commonMistakes: Adding only the single row (8 | 12 | 18 | 27 → 9,207).

questions.question: Find √15,129.
questions.explanation: It ends in 9, so the root ends in 3 or 7. Dropping two digits leaves 151, and 12² = 144 ≤ 151 < 169 = 13², so the root is 123 or 127. 125² = 15,625 > 15,129, so it is 123.
questions.method: Unit digit, bracket, midpoint.

hints.text: Drop the last two digits; the largest square up to 151 is 12².
Compare 15,129 with 125².

commonMistakes: Using only the first digit (1) for the bracket and getting a two-digit root.

questions.question: What is 1,006²?
questions.explanation: 1,006 is 6 above 1,000. Left part 1,006 + 6 = 1,012; right part 6² = 36, written as three digits: 036. So 1,006² = 10,12,036.
questions.method: Base 1,000: right part has three digits.

hints.text: Base 1,000 means the right part needs three digits.
Left part: 1,006 + 6.

commonMistakes: Writing 36 as two digits (1,01,236).
Forgetting to add the surplus to the left part (10,06,036).

questions.question: What is ∛6,58,503?
questions.explanation: The cube ends in 3, so the root ends in 7. The part before the last three digits is 658, and 8³ = 512 ≤ 658 < 729 = 9³, so the tens digit is 8. The root is 87.
questions.method: Unit digit, then the leading part.

hints.text: Which digit cubed ends in 3?
Find the cubes on either side of 658.

commonMistakes: Choosing 83 by keeping the unit digit 3.

questions.question: You want 34³ by the row method. Which row do you start from?
questions.explanation: For 10a + b with a = 3, b = 4 the row is a³ = 27, a²b = 36, ab² = 48, b³ = 64; each term is the last times 4/3. Then the middle two are doubled and added below. (9, 12, 16 is the row for squares.)
questions.method: Recognise the four-term row for cubes.

hints.text: A cube needs four terms, not three.
Start with 3³ and multiply by 4/3 each step.

commonMistakes: Using the three-term square row.

questions.question: Find 9,995².
questions.explanation: Use the base 10,000: 9,995 is 5 below. Left part 9,995 − 5 = 9,990; right part 5² = 25 written as four digits, 0025. So 9,995² = 9,99,00,025.
questions.method: Base method with a four-digit right part.

hints.text: Which base is 9,995 close to?
With base 10,000 the right part has four digits.

commonMistakes: Writing 25 with only two digits (9,99,025).

questions.question: Find √97,344.
questions.explanation: It ends in 4, so the root ends in 2 or 8. Dropping two digits leaves 973, and 31² = 961 ≤ 973 < 1,024 = 32², so the root is 312 or 318. 315² = 99,225 > 97,344, so the root is 312.
questions.method: Same three steps; the bracket now needs a two-digit k.

hints.text: After dropping two digits, 973 is left. Which square is just below it?
31² = 961. Now compare with 315².

commonMistakes: Choosing 318 without the midpoint check.

questions.question: A square garden has an area of 1,849 m². Each side is extended by 7 m. By how many square metres does the area increase?
questions.explanation: √1,849 = 43 (ends in 9 → 3 or 7; 18 → k = 4; 45² = 2,025 > 1,849). The new side is 50 m, so the new area is 2,500 m² and the increase is 2,500 − 1,849 = 651 m².
questions.method: Root first, then square the new side.

hints.text: Find the side from the area first.
√1,849 = 43, so the new side is 50 m.

commonMistakes: Adding 7² = 49 to the area, as if the increase were only the corner square.

questions.question: A cubical tank holds 4,21,875 cm³ of water when full. What is the length of its edge?
questions.explanation: The volume ends in 5, so the edge ends in 5. Dropping three digits leaves 421, and 7³ = 343 ≤ 421 < 512 = 8³, so the tens digit is 7. Edge = 75 cm.
questions.method: Cube root by unit digit and leading part.

hints.text: The edge is the cube root of the volume.
Between which two cubes does 421 lie?

commonMistakes: Choosing 65 cm by misplacing 421 between 6³ and 7³.

questions.question: Read the assertion and the reason, then choose the correct option.
questions.reason: No perfect square ends in the digit 2.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, R is false
A is false, R is true

questions.explanation: The squares of 0 to 9 end in 0, 1, 4, 9, 6, 5, 6, 9, 4, 1: never 2. So R is true, and since 8,47,602 ends in 2, R is exactly why A is true.
solutionSteps: Both true, and R explains A.
questions.method: Unit-digit test.

hints.text: List the unit digits of 0² to 9².
Does the reason, on its own, settle the assertion?

commonMistakes: Choosing "R does not explain A" when R is the whole argument.

questions.question: What is √0.000729?
questions.explanation: 0.000729 has six decimal places and 729 = 27². The root has half as many places, three: 0.027. Check: 0.027 × 0.027 = 0.000729.
questions.method: Root of the digits, half the decimal places.

hints.text: Ignore the decimal point first: what is √729?
Pair the six decimal places.

commonMistakes: Keeping six decimal places (0.000027) or using four (0.0027).

questions.question: Which of these is closest to √130?
questions.method: a + (N − a²) ÷ 2a.

hints.text: Which perfect square is nearest to 130?
Divide the gap 9 by 2 × 11.

commonMistakes: Dividing by 11 instead of 22 and getting about 11.8.

questions.question: Find √0.0441 + ∛0.008.
questions.explanation: √0.0441 = 0.21 (441 = 21², four places → two). ∛0.008 = 0.2 (8 = 2³, three places → one). The sum is 0.41.
questions.method: Square roots halve the decimal places; cube roots divide them by three.

hints.text: Handle each root separately.
For the cube root, group the three decimal places of 0.008 together.

commonMistakes: Taking ∛0.008 as 0.02.

questions.question: Select ALL the numbers that cannot be perfect squares.
questions.explanation: 36,000 ends in three zeros (an odd number). 4,375 ends in 5 but not in 25. 1,526 has digit sum 14 → 5, and a square’s digital root is 1, 4, 7 or 9. The others are squares: 2,02,500 = 450² and 7,744 = 88².
questions.method: Run each test until one fails.

hints.text: Count the zeros at the end of each number.
A square that ends in 5 must end in 25; also try the digital root.

commonMistakes: Passing 1,526 because it ends in 6, without checking the digital root.

questions.question: What is √2,000, correct to one decimal place?
questions.method: Use the nearest square, even if it is above N.

hints.text: Which perfect square is closest to 2,000?

commonMistakes: Adding the correction when the square is above N (45.3).

questions.question: What is √(3 22/49)?
questions.method: Improper fraction first, then root of top and bottom.

hints.text: Turn the mixed number into an improper fraction first.
Is the new numerator a perfect square?

commonMistakes: Taking roots of 3 and 22/49 separately.
Rooting only the numerator (13/49).
